content: Always consult your healthcare professional for comprehensive information about this medication and how it relates to your specific health needs. This medication contains glucagon, a natural substance produced by the body that raises blood sugar levels by prompting the liver to release stored sugar. It is used to treat severe low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) that requires assistance from others. Additionally, glucagon may be administered prior to certain gastrointestinal X-ray procedures. When using this medication, carefully read the Patient Information Leaflet and Instructions for Use provided by your pharmacist, both when you first receive the medication and with each refill. Caregivers should be familiar with the symptoms of low blood sugar, such as sweating, shaking, rapid heartbeat, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, or tingling in the hands or feet, and should know how to administer glucagon if necessary. Before use, visually inspect the product for particles or discoloration; do not use the liquid if either is present. Administer the medication as directed by your doctor, either into a muscle or under the skin. Dosage is determined by age, and for children, it is also based on weight. If the individual receiving glucagon is unconscious, position them on their side to prevent choking in case of vomiting. Once the person regains consciousness and can swallow, provide a quick source of sugar, such as glucose tablets or juice. Be aware that glucagon’s effects are temporary, and low blood sugar may recur. Contact your doctor immediately after an episode of severe hypoglycemia. Common side effects may include nausea, vomiting, headache, or irritation, redness, or swelling at the injection site. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Serious allergic reactions to this medication are rare. If you experience any side effects, contact your doctor for medical advice. Before using glucagon, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. Some products may contain inactive ingredients, such as latex, which can cause allergic reactions or other issues. Low blood sugar is more likely to occur if you do not consume enough calories or engage in unusually strenuous exercise. To prevent low blood sugar, eat meals on a regular schedule and avoid skipping meals. It is also advisable to carry glucose tablets or gel to treat low blood sugar. If these are unavailable, consume a quick source of sugar, such as sugar, honey, candy, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Notify your doctor immediately about any reactions and the use of this product. It is unknown whether this medication passes into breast milk, but it is unlikely to harm a nursing infant. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. In the event of an overdose with serious symptoms such as unconsciousness or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Learn to recognize the symptoms of high and low blood sugar and how to treat low blood sugar effectively. Different brands of this medication may have varying storage requirements. Refer to the product packaging or consult your pharmacist for specific storage instructions. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Your medical condition may lead to complications in an emergency. This information was last revised in August 2024. Note that this summary does not include all possible details about this product and does not guarantee that it is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always seek personalized medical advice from your healthcare professional.
